newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: PARLIAMENTARIAN QUITS SLOVAK RULING PARTY.
newsitem.headline: PARLIAMENTARIAN QUITS SLOVAK RULING PARTY.

text.p: Frantisek Gaulieder, a parliamentarian for Slovakia's ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) said on Tuesday he was quitting the party club to protest lack of democracy in Slovakia.
"There are facts (in Slovakia) which simply have nothing to do with the building of a democratic society," Gaulieder said at the beginning of a session of parliament.
"We should simply give straight answers to questions of why is transparent privatisation untransparent, why and to whom we sell shares of strategic companies for ludicrous prices," he said.

Gaulieder, who had a reputation as a dissident and critic within the HZDS of Premier Vladimir Meciar, was referring to several recent cases of the state sell-off of large companies such as oil refiner Slovnaft and oil and gas storage company Nafta at prices far below their listed share prices to groups or individuals of unknown pedigrees.

His defection from the HZDS will reduce its number of deputies to 60 in the 150-seat parliament, but will have no impact on the ruling coalition of the HZDS, the ultra-right Slovak National Party (SNS) and the ultra- left Workers' Party, which together hold 81 seats, following the defection earlier this year of a ZRS deputy.
He willo stay on in parliament as an independent.

Gaulieder, who is also a member of the parliamentary committee supervising Slovakia's SIS secret service said another reason for his defection was lack of progress in solving criminal cases with alleged SIS involvement.
"Why are we unable to solve serious crimes and why do some cases remain a mystery," Gaulieder asked his fellow parliamentarians.

He was referring to the case of Michal Kovac Junior, adult son of President Michal Kovac, was kidnapped in August 1995, when he was bundled into the boot of his car and dumped outside a police station in Austria.

Two state detectives were sacked after saying their investigations led them to suspect the involvement of the state secret service (SIS) in Kovac Junior's abduction. A third investigator in May adjourned the case due to lack of evidence.

Former policeman Robert Remias was killed in a car blast this spring after acting as the only contact between a former SIS member who said the abduction was organised by Ivan Lexa, the SIS head and close ally of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar who is locked in a bitter political feud with the president.
The police also adjourned the case of Remias death due to lack of evidence, after it said the blast had been caused by an unspecified explosive set up inside the car.
Last month U.S. ambassador to Slovakia Ralph Johnson warned Bratislava that abandoning sensitive criminal probes could damage Slovak ambitions of joining "western structures".
The U.S., the European Union and the European Parliament have recently repeated their concerns over Slovakia's foot-dragging in implementing democratic reforms.
Johnson's remarks were dismissed by Slovak foreign minister Pavol Hamzik as those from one of many ambassadors accredited to Bratislava, which earned him a rebuke from Gaulieder.

"Why do we insult foreign diplomats, why do we adopt anti-constitutional laws," Gaulider said also referring to several controversial laws rammed through by the coalition only to be later quashed by the constitutional court or returned by the president.
